metadata.title: Child poverty and academic skills at the national level: A longitudinal analysis of four waves of PISA

survey_design.weight_fields_interpretation: This study uses PISA national-level outcomes (means and proficiency-level percentages) obtained from OECD-published reports rather than analyzing individual student microdata. The authors explicitly state that they do not analyze or handle individual-level data and rely on OECD’s plausible value methodology and appropriate weights for producing the national estimates. Because the analysis is conducted at the nation-year level using pooled time-series with two-way fixed effects, student-level sampling weights and replicate weights are not directly applied in the authors’ regression stage. As a result, the weighting relevant to PISA scaling is handled upstream by the OECD, while the authors’ own models treat the OECD national estimates as given inputs.

data.handling_not_reported_explanation: The dependent variables are nation-year aggregates (PISA national means and proficiency-level percentages) taken from OECD reports, not student-level plausible-value draws. Plausible values are therefore not re-estimated or combined by the authors in their own modeling stage. For missing child poverty data, the authors describe interpolation/averaging procedures for some nation-years, but they do not report a formal missing-data handling method for the full analytic dataset in the sense of a statistical imputation framework (e.g., multiple imputation), so the missing-data handling is treated as not reported for the purposes of this schema.

sample_details.sample_filtering_criteria: The analytic dataset is constructed at the nation-year level by pooling four PISA waves (2009, 2012, 2015, 2018) and linking them to OECD/UN child poverty rates. The authors include only the 40 nations for which child poverty data are available across all four PISA waves; they exclude the remaining 16 nations that participated in all four PISA waves but lacked child poverty data. For the included 40 nations, they further handle missing child poverty values by interpolating missing years using available annual data (and, for a handful of nation-years, averaging the nearest prior and subsequent rates). They exclude Spain from reading analyses only (reducing reading N from 160 to 159 nation-years) due to concerns about implausible responses on reading assessments.

main_findings.performance_metrics: Two-way fixed-effects pooled time-series (robust SEs), N=159 nation-years. Child poverty coefficient: -0.843 (p<.05). Within-nation R²: 0.118.
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using PISA 2009/2012/2015/2018 (nation-level) Reading mean the study leveraged Child poverty rate, GDP per capita, and Total population to model Reading mean score, finding that higher child poverty is associated with lower reading mean scores within nations over time. This indicates that reducing child poverty may improve national reading achievement levels, though the fixed-effects design remains correlational and cannot fully rule out all time-varying confounding.

main_findings.target_variable: Percentage of low-skilled students in reading
main_findings.performance_metrics: Two-way fixed-effects pooled time-series (robust SEs), N=159 nation-years. Child poverty coefficient: +0.266 (p<.10). Within-nation R²: 0.159.
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using PISA 2009/2012/2015/2018 (nation-level) Reading proficiency distribution the study leveraged Child poverty rate, GDP per capita, and Total population to predict the percentage of low-skilled students in reading, finding that increases in child poverty are associated with a higher share of low-skilled students within nations over time. This indicates that child poverty reduction could be a lever for shrinking the bottom tail of reading skills, even if the study does not identify the specific mechanisms linking poverty to test performance.

main_findings.target_variable: Percentage of high-skilled students in reading
main_findings.performance_metrics: Two-way fixed-effects pooled time-series (robust SEs), N=159 nation-years. Child poverty coefficient: -0.041 (not significant). Within-nation R²: 0.168.
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using PISA 2009/2012/2015/2018 (nation-level) Reading proficiency distribution the study leveraged Child poverty rate, GDP per capita, and Total population to predict the percentage of high-skilled students in reading, finding that child poverty does not have a statistically detectable association with the high-skilled share within nations over time. This indicates that poverty-focused policies may primarily affect the lower end of reading skills rather than the top end, though the null result could reflect limited statistical power or unmeasured time-varying factors.

main_findings.performance_metrics: Two-way fixed-effects pooled time-series (robust SEs), N=160 nation-years. Child poverty coefficient: -1.030 (p<.05). Within-nation R²: 0.115.
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using PISA 2009/2012/2015/2018 (nation-level) Math mean the study leveraged Child poverty rate, GDP per capita, and Total population to model Math mean score, finding that higher child poverty is associated with lower math mean scores within nations over time. This indicates that national strategies to reduce child poverty may raise overall math achievement levels, while causality cannot be confirmed because the analysis does not fully account for all time-varying educational resource changes.

main_findings.target_variable: Percentage of low-skilled students in math
main_findings.performance_metrics: Two-way fixed-effects pooled time-series (robust SEs), N=160 nation-years. Child poverty coefficient: +0.305 (p<.05). Within-nation R²: 0.083.
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using PISA 2009/2012/2015/2018 (nation-level) Math proficiency distribution the study leveraged Child poverty rate, GDP per capita, and Total population to predict the percentage of low-skilled students in math, finding that increases in child poverty are associated with a higher share of low-skilled students within nations over time. This indicates that poverty reduction may be particularly important for preventing math skill deficits among the lowest-performing students, though the study’s fixed-effects approach still leaves room for residual confounding.

main_findings.target_variable: Percentage of high-skilled students in math
main_findings.performance_metrics: Two-way fixed-effects pooled time-series (robust SEs), N=160 nation-years. Child poverty coefficient: -0.270 (p<.05). Within-nation R²: 0.204.
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using PISA 2009/2012/2015/2018 (nation-level) Math proficiency distribution the study leveraged Child poverty rate, GDP per capita, and Total population to predict the percentage of high-skilled students in math, finding that higher child poverty is associated with a lower share of high-skilled students within nations over time. This indicates that child poverty reduction may help protect top-end math performance, suggesting broader benefits beyond the bottom tail, while the study does not directly test the causal pathways.

main_findings.performance_metrics: Two-way fixed-effects pooled time-series (robust SEs), N=160 nation-years. Child poverty coefficient: -1.030 (p<.001). Within-nation R²: 0.420.
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using PISA 2009/2012/2015/2018 (nation-level) Science mean the study leveraged Child poverty rate, GDP per capita, and Total population to model Science mean score, finding that higher child poverty is associated with lower science mean scores within nations over time. This indicates that reducing child poverty may improve national science achievement, though the analysis remains observational and cannot fully isolate poverty’s effect from other contemporaneous policy and resource changes.

main_findings.target_variable: Percentage of low-skilled students in science
main_findings.performance_metrics: Two-way fixed-effects pooled time-series (robust SEs), N=160 nation-years. Child poverty coefficient: +0.358 (p<.001). Within-nation R²: 0.462.
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using PISA 2009/2012/2015/2018 (nation-level) Science proficiency distribution the study leveraged Child poverty rate, GDP per capita, and Total population to predict the percentage of low-skilled students in science, finding that increases in child poverty are associated with a higher share of low-skilled students within nations over time. This indicates that child poverty reduction could be an effective strategy for lowering the prevalence of low science proficiency, while the study does not identify the specific educational or social mechanisms involved.

main_findings.target_variable: Percentage of high-skilled students in science
main_findings.performance_metrics: Two-way fixed-effects pooled time-series (robust SEs), N=160 nation-years. Child poverty coefficient: +0.013 (not significant). Within-nation R²: 0.912.
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using PISA 2009/2012/2015/2018 (nation-level) Science proficiency distribution the study leveraged Child poverty rate, GDP per capita, and Total population to predict the percentage of high-skilled students in science, finding that child poverty does not show a statistically significant association with the high-skilled share within nations over time. This indicates that poverty-related disadvantages may be more consequential for preventing low proficiency in science than for reducing top-end science performance, though the very high R² suggests strong time-trend structure that may mask other effects.

data.outcome_summary: The study links OECD/UN child poverty rates to national PISA outcomes across four waves (2009, 2012, 2015, 2018), analyzing 40 nations (N=160 nation-years; N=159 for reading after excluding Spain from reading due to implausible responses). Using pooled time-series two-way fixed-effects models with nation and year controls, the authors find that within-nation increases in child poverty are associated with lower mean academic skills in reading, math, and science (e.g., reading mean: −0.843; math mean: −1.030; science mean: −1.030). Child poverty also increases the share of low-skilled students in all three subjects (reading: +0.266; math: +0.305; science: +0.358). For high-skilled students, the association is negative for math only (−0.270) and not significant for reading or science. The analysis is correlational despite fixed effects, and child poverty missingness is handled via interpolation/averaging rather than a fully specified statistical imputation framework.
